summary: Suggests a simple way for delivering wireless messages, one-way and two-way, to appropriate receiving devices such as pagers. It describes version 3 of the Simple Network Paging Protocol. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A simple set of rules for sending a short message to someone's pager.

questions: how to send a page over the internet
how does the simple network paging protocol work
what does snpp level 3 two-way do
why not use email for paging
subtitle: A line-based, SMTP-like protocol for pushing a page to a paging terminal and, in version 3, getting replies back.

tldr.problem: Delivering an alphanumeric page meant modems and phone lines and the awkward TAP/IXO protocol, and email could not tell a sender quickly that delivery had failed.
tldr.mechanism: SNPP is a text conversation over a network connection: the client names a pager, supplies a message and says SEND, and the server answers every command with a three-digit code. Level 2 adds options, and level 3 adds two-way acknowledgments and replies.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo describing gateways the author says were already in use, and it replaces RFC 1645. Reviewers had preferred an email-based approach.

facts.label: Message end marker
facts.value: a single period on its own line

today: RFC 1861 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1645 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It is not an Internet standard, and the text states the IETF reviewers preferred an email-based approach.

sections.title: Why a Separate Paging Protocol
sections.content:
The Simple Network Paging Protocol (SNPP) aims to let pages be delivered to paging terminals over the Internet, removing the need for modems and phone lines to produce alphanumeric pages. Most pages reach a terminal through TAP (Telocator Alphanumeric input Protocol, also called IXO), which the RFC calls convoluted, with old-style ASCII control characters and a non-standard checksum. A newer standard, TME, was expected, and the level 2 features are meant for it. At publication the RFC notes that TME was still not finalized.

The RFC argues that email is the wrong tool for urgent pages. Mail can be deferred for hours with no notice to the sender, while an SNPP session shows a problem at once. A separate protocol also lets the sender control exactly what reaches the pager, instead of header lines that waste radio bandwidth. For two-way paging, the unpredictable time a subscriber takes to answer makes phone-line sessions costly, so the Internet is attractive.
sections.plainLanguage: If you mail a letter and the post office is closed, you will not find out for hours. If you phone instead, you know straight away. SNPP is the phone call for pager messages.

sections.title: How a Session Works
sections.content:
SNPP is a sequence of commands and replies, in the style of other Internet protocols. The first four characters of each command are significant. The client opens a connection and the server greets it with a 220 message. The client supplies a pager ID and a message, then sends SEND. The server hands the page to the paging terminal, gathers a response and reports success or failure.

The first digit of every reply code gives its category: 2xx success, 3xx begin DATA input, 4xx failure with the connection terminated, 5xx failure but the session continues. Version 3 adds 7xx (unsuccessful two-way transaction, session continues), 8xx (successful two-way transaction) and 9xx (successful queued two-way transaction). The text after the code may be changed to suit the operator, and the RFC suggests mirroring SMTP codes closely. A 550 signals an administrative failure such as a bad pager ID, while 554 signals a technical one. A server may also apply an inactivity timeout, answering 421 Timeout, Goodbye.
sections.plainLanguage: You and the server take turns. You say something, and the server answers with a number that tells you at a glance whether things are fine or something went wrong.

sections.title: Level 1: The Minimum Commands
sections.content:
Level 1 is the minimum implementation and works with either TAP/IXO or TME behind it. PAGEr submits a pager ID, which must be known to the paging terminal; the server may check basics such as length, but real validation may only happen when the page is sent. MESSage gives a single-line message. SEND finalizes the transaction. If the pager or message is missing, the server should reply 503 and let the user continue; otherwise it formats the page and sends it to the terminal. After a send, the server should stay online for another transaction.

RESEt clears everything entered so far, as if the connection were fresh. QUIT ends the session with 221 OK, Goodbye. HELP is optional and returns lines prefixed 214, ended by a 250 message.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic steps are: say who, say what, say send. There are also buttons to start over and to hang up.

sections.title: Level 2: Optional Extensions
sections.content:
Level 2 adds DATA, a multi-line alternative to MESSage. The server answers 354, the client sends lines, and a single period alone at the start of a line ends the input, much like SMTP's DATA command. Only one of DATA or MESSage may be used before a SEND.

The remaining level 2 commands mirror features of TME, and no server is required to implement all of them. Unsupported ones should return 500. They include LOGIn (anonymous status is assumed without it), a PAGEr form that takes a password or PIN, LEVEl (service level 0 to 11, with 1 as normal), ALERt (0 do not alert, 1 alert), COVErage (an alternate coverage area), HOLDuntil (delayed delivery), CALLerid and SUBJect.

These options work in an option-option-option-go style: set the options, then issue PAGEr, after which the options reset to defaults. That lets one message go to two people with different priorities or coverage areas.
sections.plainLanguage: Level 2 adds extras, like writing a longer note, picking how urgent it is, choosing which area to page, or asking for the message to arrive later.

sections.title: Level 3: Two-Way Paging
sections.content:
Level 3 supports acknowledgment-based paging such as ReFLEX. A transaction starts with 2WAY and ends with SEND or RESEt. Within it, PING locates a unit and reports its status (a subscriber may choose a generic reply that hides location), NOQUEUEing refuses queuing if the unit is offline, EXPTag sets how many hours a queued message lives, and ACKRead asks the unit to report when the subscriber actually views the message.

RTYPe sets the reply type: NONE (the default), YESNO, SIMREPLY, MULTICHOICE or TEXT. With MCREsponse the sender seeds a message with multiple-choice answers, each with a 2-byte code. A successful SEND returns a Message_Tag, which works as a record locator, and a Pass_Code, a random PIN. The client then polls with MSTAtus to follow progress, and KTAG deletes the tag when finished.

Reply codes show how final the transaction is: 86x initial message delivered, 87x intermediate processing done, 88x transaction concluded (no more changes), 96x queued. For example 881 means delivered and read, and 888 means a multiple-choice reply was received.
sections.plainLanguage: With two-way pagers the other person can answer. You get a claim ticket when you send, and you can check back to see whether the message arrived, was read, and what they picked as their answer.

sections.title: History, IETF Review and Security
sections.content:
The first proposal used POP2-style result codes; the community asked for numeric codes like SMTP, and the protocol was changed. Administrative errors (550) were separated from technical ones (554). Level 2 was added ahead of TME deployment and level 3 ahead of acknowledgment-based messaging.

The IETF working group and three IESG members who reviewed the work concluded that an approach using existing email infrastructure was preferable, given the high cost of deploying a new protocol. Some thought SMTP extensions would do. The author still believed a separate protocol had merit, to isolate TAP/IXO details from users and from mail-based approaches. On security, the RFC says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: Some experts said to use ordinary email instead of a new system. The author thought a special pager system was still worth having, and he wrote this down so people could judge for themselves.
